title: Three Domains of Feedback: Linguistic, Communicative, and Affective
brief: Open by establishing the three domains the module identifies: linguistic feedback (focused on language accuracy), communicative feedback (focused on the task or message content), and affective feedback (building learner confidence and encouraging attempts to communicate). Draw directly on the Module 5 Introduction's expanded narrative, which states that 'incorrectness is not the only standard teachers can use to assess learning.' Explain why all three domains matter in a balanced feedback routine, and note that the module's primary focus is formative feedback — continuous feedback given at all stages of learning — rather than summative feedback given at the end of a unit. Briefly acknowledge that research (Lyster & Saito, 2010; Li, 2010) confirms corrective feedback aids acquisition, but keep this to a single sentence so the unit stays practical rather than re-teaching the meta-analysis covered in unit 9.1.

title: General Dos and Don'ts: Installing a Feedback Mindset
brief: Cover the module's practical guidelines for deciding when and how to give feedback: understanding why an error occurred (careless mistake vs. incomplete learning), determining the type of error (grammar, vocabulary, or pragmatic), and matching feedback to both the error type and the context. Emphasise the module's explicit caution against over-correction and too much negative feedback, and its instruction to 'avoid trying to correct every error' — teachers must judge whether an error impedes understanding or whether fluency matters more for the current task. Use the module's guidance that teachers should 'tell students that making mistakes helps them learn' and create 'a comfortable atmosphere in which students see making mistakes as part of the learning process,' drawing on the answer-key narrative about the teacher who told her students directly that mistakes were natural and thereby set up an atmosphere of acceptance that led to more and better practice.

title: On-the-Spot and Delayed Oral Feedback: Practical Routines
brief: Describe the two timing options the module presents for oral feedback — immediate (on-the-spot) and delayed — and give concrete classroom examples drawn from the Video Segment 2 answer key. Explain the story-retelling example in which the teacher used gestures, restatement, question-word cues, clapping, and words of approval rather than direct negative correction, and how her feedback stayed focused on the communicative goal rather than interrupting for pronunciation or grammar details. Introduce the delayed-feedback board-slot routine: the module suggests the teacher take notes during an activity and address patterned errors with the whole class after the activity is complete, or use audio/video recordings for students to find and self-correct one or two recurring errors. Also draw on the parent-conference example from the answer key as an illustration of creative delayed feedback that increased student participation.

title: Feedback on Written Work: Techniques and Formats
brief: Walk through the module's table of writing activities and paired feedback techniques from Video Segment 3, covering the full range from accuracy-focused tasks (writing the alphabet, copying) to fluency-focused tasks (writing a story, synthesizing information for a report). Highlight the practical strategies the module recommends: providing models for comparison, having a partner read a finished copy aloud against the model, sending a letter to another student for a real response, and supplying a checklist of errors for self-checking a report. Stress the module's principle of focused feedback — when guidelines tell students exactly which points will be evaluated, correction is limited to those points — as a way to avoid overwhelming learners. Connect this to the broader guideline that feedback should 'fit both the kind of error and the context in which it occurred.'

title: Peer and Self-Assessment: Building Independent Learners
brief: Draw on the module's peer-feedback group procedure from the Video Segment 1 answer key: students grouped by learning style created activities, distributed them to other groups, then collected and checked the completed work themselves. Explain the module's reasoning that peer feedback 'can reduce overall anxiety about making mistakes' while simultaneously causing students to focus and figure out for themselves what was correct — and note the module's important caveat that the teacher must monitor such work closely to ensure feedback is both correct and helpful. Connect peer correction to the action-plan goal of helping 'students learn to self-correct in order to make them more independent learners.' Introduce self-assessment habits the module supports: using checklists, reviewing recordings, and reflecting on patterned errors, all of which shift responsibility for noticing errors gradually toward the learner.

title: Praise That Names the Behavior and Keeping Feedback Encouraging
brief: Focus on the affective dimension of feedback as a deliberate teaching tool, drawing on the module's distinction between positive feedback that rewards correct or successful communication and affective feedback whose explicit purpose is to build confidence. Use the module's concrete positive-feedback examples from the Video Segment 2 answer key — clapping, 'Very good,' 'Keep going,' thanking students, repeating a student's response to make it clear to the class — and contrast these with vague or purely evaluative praise. Explain the module's principle that the teacher's behavior must be consistent with any stated belief: if a teacher says mistakes are natural but then gives frequent negative correction, students will not believe the original statement. Close with the module's overarching guideline to 'encourage student learning through positive feedback' and help students 'be successful and confident,' framing this as the thread that holds all the practical routines in this unit together.
